To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

Show details

Some essential information could not be detected: software

power_id text
1;2 To determine the minimum required sample size, we conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the two main hypotheses (H1, H2). For both power analyses, we simulated data based on two previous studies (Huang et al., 2026; Nevejans et al., 2026) and a pilot study on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. The power analysis for H1, which concerned the correlation between performance on the DR task and on the VPT task (see below for more details), indicated that a sample size of N = 164 would allow us to detect a small correlation of r = -.25 with 90.26% power, using a significance threshold of .05. The simulation-based power analysis for H2, which concerned the correlation between performance on the DR task and the Faux Pas Recognition Test (see below for more details), indicated that N = 164 would allow us to detect a small correlation of r = .25 with 90.05% power, using a significance threshold of .05. For full simulation rationale and code, and data from the pilot study on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, see

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To improve (4)

To improve Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 3 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .512 In contrast to H1, participants’ accuracy on the DR task was not significantly correlated with their relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, r(162) = .05, p = .512, 95% CI [-.10, .20].
p = .737 There was no significant heterogeneity of the effect between the two experiments, Q(1) = 0.11, p = .737.
p = .351 Contrary to the prediction based on RFT, the partial correlation between DR scores and the VPT accuracy congruency effect was non-significant after controlling for ICAR scores, r(161) = -.07, p = .351, 95% CI [-.22, .08].

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 14 distinct packages/libraries: BayesFactor, betafunctions, car, cocor, ltm, MASS, meta, performance, ppcor, psych, rstatix, scales, sirt, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 213 columns across 9 data files.

Issues Identified

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

File Column Issues
pilot study/raw/raw.csv gender_text ⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 9639 values are missing
preprocessed_deictic_relating_task.csv trial_num #️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 92% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: “XX”
processed_pilot.csv gender_text ⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 99 values are missing

Careless Responding

6 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 6 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

Respondent Blocks flagged Scales Longest run Short-scale only
42 1 aq (1-4, 6 items) same answer 6 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5) yes
77 1 aq (1-4, 6 items) same answer 6 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5) yes
90 1 aq (1-4, 6 items) same answer 6 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5) yes
1 1 aq (1-4, 6 items) same answer 5 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5) yes
25 1 aq (1-4, 6 items) same answer 5 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5) yes
69 1 aq (1-4, 6 items) same answer 5 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5) yes

What this does not cover. Only 1 of 9 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • power_simulation.R reads deictic_task.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • analysis_confirmatory.R: cortest_icar

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • processing.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • preprocessing.qmd

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 30 statistical tests reported in the paper, 10 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 9 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 power_simulation.R — none
2 preprocessing.qmd — none
3 processing_pilot.qmd — none
4 processing.qmd preprocessing.qmd dependency
5 processing.R preprocessing.qmd dependency
6 analysis_confirmatory.qmd processing.qmd, processing.R dependency
7 analysis_confirmatory.R processing.qmd, processing.R, analysis_confirmatory.qmd dependency
8 analysis_meta_analysis.qmd processing.qmd, processing.R dependency
9 analysis_posthoc.qmd processing.qmd, processing.R dependency

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 3 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: deictic_task.csv, vpt_task_simdata.csv, pilot_fauxpas_task.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 9 scripts: 5 ran without error, 3 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: analysis_confirmatory.R after analysis_confirmatory.qmd. Such a script should source() the other itself, since it does not run on its own. A script looked for a file in another folder than the deposit has it, so before running it once more we copied it there: pilot study/raw/raw.csv to data/raw/raw.csv for preprocessing.qmd. Building paths from the top of the project (as with here::here()), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

a script hit an object '...' not found error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

> alpha.strat.ci <- function(data, itemstrata_data, sims){
>    
>    # we bootstrap: compute stratified alpha for the number of dataframes defined in sims (e.g., create 5 (= sims) dataframes based on data and compute stratified alpha)
>    alpha_strats <- replicate(sims, {
>       n = dim(data)[1]
>       data_booted <- data[sample(1:n, replace = TRUE), ]
>       stratified_full <- as.data.frame(sirt::stratified.cronbach.alpha(data = data_booted, itemstrata = itemstrata_data))
>       strati <- stratified_full$alpha.stratified[1]
>    })
>    
>    # compute stratified alpha for specific dataset
>    stratified_alpha = sirt::stratified.cronbach.alpha(data = data, itemstrata=itemstrata_data)$alpha.stratified[1]
>    
>    # define bootstrapped 95CI based
>    bootstrap_95ci_low = quantile(alpha_strats, probs = c(0.025))
>    bootstrap_95ci_high = quantile(alpha_strats, probs = c(0.975))
>    
>    # And combine it into one
>    return(round(data.frame(stratified_alpha, bootstrap_95ci_low, bootstrap_95ci_high,
>                            row.names = ""), 2))
> }

> corrected_vpt_splitHalf <- function(sims = 1){
>    
>    corrected_corsplits <- replicate(sims, { # this is the simulation
>       
>       vpt_with_ranrow <- vpt_processed.df %>% 
>          # We order the full task based on conditions, to get a balanced split-sample of trials (= conditions in each half)
>          select(pp_number, vpt_angle, vpt_congruency, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_pos_red, vpt_distance, vpt_trial_number, vpt_trial_accuracy, duration) %>%
>          arrange(pp_number, vpt_distance, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_congruency, vpt_trial_number) %>% # arrange the rows per condition
>          group_by(pp_number, vpt_distance, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_congruency) %>%
>          mutate(row_random = sample(row_number(), replace = F)) %>% # give each row a number within each relevant condition
>          arrange(pp_number, vpt_distance, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_congruency, row_random) %>%
>          mutate(split = ifelse(row_random %% 2 == 0, 2, 1)) # odd numbers in one half, even in the other; somewhat equal halves
>       
>       vtp_split1 <- vpt_with_ranrow %>% filter(split == 1) # one half 
>       
>       vtp_split2 <- vpt_with_ranrow %>% filter(split == 2) # another half
>       
>       # And calculate the congruency effect for each split (same code as above)
>       rce_s1 <- vtp_split1 %>%
>          group_by(pp_number,
>                   vpt_angle, vpt_congruency, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_pos_red, vpt_distance) %>% # congruency within different conditions
>          summarise(marginal_rt = mean(duration)) %>%
>          group_by(pp_number, vpt_congruency) %>%
>          summarise(mean_rt = mean(marginal_rt)) %>%
>          spread(vpt_congruency, mean_rt) %>%
>          mutate(vpt_rel_ce_rt = (incongruent - congruent)/((incongruent+congruent)/2)) %>% # we divide by the average speed for each participant
>          ungroup() %>%
>          select(pp_number, vpt_rel_ce_rt) 
>       
>       rce_s2 <- vtp_split2 %>%
>          group_by(pp_number,
>                   vpt_angle, vpt_congruency, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_pos_red, vpt_distance) %>% # congruency within different conditions
>          summarise(marginal_rt = mean(duration)) %>%
>          group_by(pp_number, vpt_congruency) %>%
>          summarise(mean_rt = mean(marginal_rt)) %>%
>          spread(vpt_congruency, mean_rt) %>%
>          mutate(vpt_rel_ce_rt = (incongruent - congruent)/((incongruent+congruent)/2)) %>% # we divide by the average speed for each participant
>          ungroup() %>%
>          select(pp_number, vpt_rel_ce_rt) 
>       
>       #Finally, we correlate the congruency effects in these splits, and Spearman-Brown correct it 
>       cor_splits <- cor(rce_s1$vpt_rel_ce_rt, rce_s2$vpt_rel_ce_rt, method = "pearson")
>       
>       corrected_split_cor <- (2*cor_splits)/(1 + cor_splits) #Spearman-Brown corrected
>       corrected_split_cor
>       
>    })
>    
>    quantile(corrected_corsplits, probs = c(0.025, 0.50, 0.975)) # from the lest of correlations, take these values
> }
> corrected_vpt_splitHalf(sims = 10000)

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants were native English speakers, recruited via Prolific Academic.

Based on the given premises and reversal statement, participants had to select all buttons with true or false statements from 2-to-4 buttons.

Trials differed based on whether participants had to indicate true or false statements, the number of buttons (2, 3, 4), and the number of true (none true, one true, two true) vs. false (none false, one false, two false, three false) statements.

If participants had not clicked the submit button before the response deadline of 80 seconds, no response was registered, and the next trial started immediately.

There was no response deadline, but participants were instructed to react as fast and accurately as possible.

At the start of the study, participants provided informed consent and demographic information, including age and gender (“male,” “female,” “non-binary,” “not listed,” or “prefer not to say”).

After the DR task, participants completed the VPT task and Faux Pas Recognition Test, for which the order was randomized across participants.

After both tasks, participants completed the ICAR Sample Test and the AQ-Short.

Finally, participants were debriefed and informed that they could contact the researcher via Prolific if they had any questions or would like to receive a summary of the results.

Participants were also given the option to leave a comment before finishing the study.

Eight participants were excluded because they failed more than one out of the four attention checks during the experiment.

Four additional participants were excluded because they had more than 20% trials with RTs ≤ 5 seconds during the DR task (1 participant) or because their average accuracy in the VPT task was ≤ 57% (3 participants).

Participants had an average score of 60.47% (SD = 24.39%) on the DR task.

Participants were faster (Mraw RT difference = 358 ms, SD = 527 ms) and more accurate (Mdifference = 6.75%, SD = 9.59%) on congruent compared to incongruent trials.

Participants had an average accuracy of 55.26% (SD = 19.69%) on the ICAR Sample Test.

In our previous research using Prolific samples, up to 11% of participants also scored above the 50-item AQ cut-off (Nevejans et al., 2026; Experiment 1), suggesting a possible selection bias toward individuals with elevated autism traits on Prolific, at least for this type of research.

After each block, participants were informed about their average accuracy in the finished block.

Ethics approval statement:

Ethical approval was granted by the ethical committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences at Ghent University with reference number 2025-091A.
