How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

We try to exclude figure and table notes like “* p < .05”, but may not succeed at excluding all false positives.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Relational Frame Theory (RFT) proposes that deictic relating plays a critical role in "Theory of Mind" (ToM). However, empirical research to date on the relationship between deictic relating and ToM has been inconclusive, potentially due to small sample sizes and limitations in the assessment of deictic relating. In the present online study (N = 164), we tested the relationship between deictic relating and two ToM measures: a low-level ToM task (a visual perspective-taking task) and a high-level ToM task (the Faux Pas Recognition Test).

We additionally tested associations with general cognitive ability and autism traits. Based on predictions from RFT, we hypothesized that deictic relating would correlate with both ToM measures, with a stronger association for low-level ToM. We observed a positive correlation of deictic relating with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, whereas its correlation with visual perspective-taking was non-significant for our primary outcome measure.

Opposite to predictions derived from RFT, deictic relating was positively correlated with autism traits, whereas scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test and visual perspective-taking task were not significantly correlated with autism traits. Although these findings may suggest a relationship between deictic relating and ToM, the absence of an association with low-level ToM is difficult to reconcile with RFT. Alternative explanations for observed correlations, including task characteristics or other related abilities, are discussed. Finally, the finding that higher scores on the autism traits questionnaire were related to better deictic relating is at odds with RFT and raises questions about which abilities the task measures.

[div-01]

Theory of Mind (ToM), typically defined as the ability to attribute mental states to oneself and others (Premack & Woodruff, 1978), is argued to be crucial for successful social interaction (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Leslie et al., 2004; Long et al., 2025; Todd & Galinsky, 2014). ToM has been investigated in many subfields of cognitive psychology (Schaafsma et al., 2015) and can therefore be seen as an "umbrella term" encompassing several related abilities. Howlin et al. (1999) classified these ToM abilities into five developmental levels of increasing complexity. The first two levels, simple and complex visual perspective-taking (VPT), reflect the understanding that different people can see different things (level 1) or the same thing differently (level 2). Level 3 refers to the understanding that individuals can only know what they have (in)directly experienced, also named "seeing leads to knowing". Finally, levels 4 and 5, considered to be the most complex ToM levels, involve predicting actions based on a person's true (level 4) or false (level 5) beliefs (Howlin et al., 1999; Montoya-Rodríguez & Cobos, 2016). However, it remains unclear whether these different abilities indeed rely on a single underlying "ToM process" or instead reflect distinct cognitive processes (Brucato et al., 2026; Quesque & Rossetti, 2020; Schaafsma et al., 2015).

Relational Frame Theory (RFT; Hayes et al., 2001) provides an alternative, behavioranalytic view of ToM abilities through the concept of deictic relating (DR), a specific type of relational responding. RFT proposes that relational responding lies at the core of human cognition and language, and distinguishes different types of relating, referred to as relational frames, such as frames of coordination (e.g., A is the same as B), opposition (e.g., A is opposite to B), or temporality (e.g., A comes after B). Perspective-taking is assumed to involve responding to a family of deictic frames, including three key deictic relations: interpersonal relations (I versus YOU), spatial relations (HERE versus THERE), and temporal relations (NOW versus THEN). According to RFT, DR develops through a history of reinforcement to responding to questions involving these critical relations, such as "What are you doing right now?", "What did you eat at school today?", or "What did your sister do this morning?" Responding to such questions requires children to distinguish their own perspective in the "here" and "now" from other perspectives, including those of another person (e.g., "their sister"), at a different place (e.g., "at school"), and at a different time (e.g., "this morning"). Repeatedly making such distinctions across contexts allows children to abstract the underlying relational properties, through which they learn to describe their own perspective in relation to others (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; McHugh et al., 2004; Rehfeldt et al., 2007). RFT researchers have claimed that DR represents the essential behavioral repertoire for ToM abilities described in cognitive psychology (Hempkin et al., 2024), although some claim that, whereas DR would be heavily involved in levels 1-to-3 of ToM, higher levels (and especially false-belief reasoning) might involve more than DR, such as logical-not reasoning (e.g., "you were NOT here"; Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004) or relating of relational networks (Kavanagh et al., 2020).

Based on the assumed link between DR and ToM, several studies within RFT have tested whether training individuals on DR also improves performance on ToM tasks, with the aim of eventually applying such training to populations thought to experience ToM difficulties, such as individuals with autismfoot_0 (Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014). To do so, researchers typically use the so-called "Barnes-Holmes protocol" (see McHugh et al., 2004) to assess and train DR across three levels of relational complexity: simple, reversed, and double reversed.

In each trial of this protocol, the researcher gives the participant certain information involving deictic relations, such as "I am sitting here on the black chair and you are sitting there on the blue chair," after which the participant must answer two questions, for example, "Where am I sitting? Where are you sitting?" Crucially, deictic relational information can be "reversed" in certain trials through an additional statement, such as "If I were you and you were me" (an interpersonal reversal). A double reversal statement, considered to have the highest relational complexity, could be "If now were then and then were now, and if here were there and there were here", in which both the temporal and spatial deictic relations are reversed (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Rehfeldt et al., 2007).

Studies using the Barnes-Holmes protocol to investigate transfer of DR training to ToM task performance have, however, provided mixed results. Some studies reported (descriptive) improvements on level 3 to 5 ToM tasks following DR training in typically developing children (Weil et al., 2011), adolescents with autism (Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014), and adults with schizophrenia (O'Neill & Weil, 2014). However, other studies have found no such improvements on ToM tests across all five levels in typically developing children (Montoya-Rodríguez & Cobos, 2016) or children with autism (Jackson et al., 2014).

Importantly, all these studies had very small sample sizes, with no more than three participants in the training group, and relied on descriptive comparisons of accuracy scores rather than statistical inference tests. Although behavior analysis has historically used such descriptive analyses informatively, this is in the context of single-case experimental designs; the above studies, by contrast, largely focus on designs that are closer to typical group-level approaches, which are less appropriate for such descriptive analyses (Cummins, 2026). More recently, Taylor et al. (2023) addressed these limitations by recruiting a larger adult sample and including an active control group. They found no transfer of DR training to performance on a VPT task, nor to an implicit relational assessment procedure intended to measure perspective-taking within an RFT framework. A recent scoping review on the relationship between ToM and DR in autism reached a similar conclusion, stating that there is currently insufficient evidence for improvements in ToM performance after DR training (Hempkin et al., 2024).

Besides training studies, others have tested correlations between DR and ToM task performance. Hendriks et al. (2016) reported significant correlations between Barnes-Holmes protocol performance and two vignette-based ToM tasks, the Faux Pas Recognition Test and Strange Stories Test, in a mixed clinical and non-clinical sample, although only the correlation with the Faux Pas Recognition Test remained significant after controlling for intelligence, and effects were limited to specific trial types in the Barnes-Holmes protocol.

Similarly, Villatte et al. (2008 Villatte et al. ( , 2010) ) found significant correlations between Barnes-Holmes protocol performance and another vignette-based ToM task, the Hinting Task, which assesses recognition of indirect requests or hints, although these associations were restricted to particular subsamples defined by schizophrenia diagnosis (Villatte et al., 2010) or anhedonia trait scores (Villatte et al., 2008).

Hence, it remains unclear whether DR is related to ToM performance, particularly in the general adult population. The current study tested the relationship between DR performance and a low-and high-level ToM task in a large adult sample, thereby addressing the limited sample sizes in most previous studies. Aside from sample size limitations, the Barnes-Holmes protocol might also be a suboptimal measure of DR performance, especially in adults. Indeed, the protocol was originally designed to train children with lower DR abilities (Kavanagh et al., 2020), and it is therefore unclear whether the protocol has sufficient variation in difficulty to assess performance in adults. To address this concern, the current study employed a recently developed DR task (Nevejans et al., 2026). This task combined the typical task format of the Barnes-Holmes protocol (McHugh et al., 2004), in which participants must reverse information based on some statements, with the structure of the Relational Abilities Index (Colbert et al., 2020; Cummins et al., 2023; J. Cummins & J. De Houwer, personal communication, June 2024), a general assessment of relational abilities in adults. In a previous study, this DR task showed good internal consistency and no ceiling effect in adults (Nevejans et al., 2026).

To assess both low-and high-level ToM, we included a level-2 VPT task (Huang et al., 2026) and the Faux Pas Recognition Test (level 5 ToM; Burghardt et al., 2025; Stone et al., 1998). We further included a measure of cognitive abilities and an assessment of autism traits. First, given that both ToM (Baker et al., 2014; Navarro et al., 2021) and DR (Gore et al., 2010) have been shown to correlate with intelligence measures, observed relationships may be (partially) driven by general cognitive ability. Therefore, we included an intelligence proxy, the International Cognitive Ability Resource (ICAR) Sample Test (Condon & Revelle, 2014), to test associations of the included tasks with cognitive ability. Second, because ToM (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Long et al., 2025) and DR (Hempkin et al., 2024; Rehfeldt et al., 2007) have been linked to autism, we included a self-report questionnaire of autism traits, the shortened version of the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-Short; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Hoekstra et al., 2011), to test the relationship between performance on the tasks and autism traits in the general population. We tested two primary hypotheses about the relationship between DR and ToM.

Based on RFT, our first primary hypothesis (H1) was that DR performance would be positively associated with VPT; our second primary hypothesis (H2) was that DR performance would be positively associated with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. However, because some theorists have argued that DR alone may be insufficient to support higher-level ToM abilities (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Kavanagh et al., 2020), we added the secondary hypothesis that DR would be more strongly associated with VPT than with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. Additionally, we tested the relationship between autism traits and performance on the DR and ToM tasks. The ToM hypothesis of autism states that individuals with autism should perform worse on ToM tasks (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985), and previous research has linked autism traits to lower ToM scores (Atherton & Cross, 2019; Gökçen et al., 2016; Nijhof et al., 2017). Based on this, we predicted a negative correlation between ToM performance and autism traits. Regarding DR and autism traits, previous work within RFT assumes that individuals with autism would perform worse on DR (Kavanagh et al., 2020; Rehfeldt et al., 2007). Based on such previous claims within RFT, we would hence expect a negative correlation between autism traits and DR performance.

However, a previous study with the novel DR task in a large general sample did not observe any correlation between autism traits and performance on DR (Nevejans et al., 2026). The current study therefore aimed to test whether the predicted negative correlation is observed or whether the previous null result is replicated.

Method Transparency and Openness

This experiment was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/zdxbn/overview?view_only=579cd1b916764fbbac3d8101e77b6c2c). The experiment code with the VPT task, DR task, Faux Pas Recognition Test, and the AQ-Short, and data and analysis files can be found on the OSF (https://osf.io/794zs/overview?view_only=3e280f4fb23f481a8ec0a5028cffa73c). Materials for the ICAR Sample Test, and the English stories from the original Faux Pas Recognition Test (Stone et al., 1998) are not shared due to copyright restrictions. We report how we determined our sample size, all participant and trial exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study (Simmons et al., 2012).

Participants

To determine the minimum required sample size, we conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the two main hypotheses (H1, H2). For both power analyses, we simulated data based on two previous studies (Huang et al., 2026; Nevejans et al., 2026) and a pilot study on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. The power analysis for H1, which concerned the correlation between performance on the DR task and on the VPT task (see below for more details), indicated that a sample size of N = 164 would allow us to detect a small correlation of r = -.25 with 90.26% power, using a significance threshold of .05. The simulation-based power analysis for H2, which concerned the correlation between performance on the DR task and the Faux Pas Recognition Test (see below for more details), indicated that N = 164 would allow us to detect a small correlation of r = .25 with 90.05% power, using a significance threshold of .05. For full simulation rationale and code, and data from the pilot study on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, see

Participants were native English speakers, recruited via Prolific Academic.

Participants who completed the study were reimbursed £9 (approximately £8 per hour) for their participation. Once 164 complete submissions had been collected, data were screened for exclusion criteria (see Analysis section), and excluded submissions were replaced through additional recruitment. This process was repeated until we obtained the preregistered sample size from the power analysis (N = 164). In total, 176 complete submissions were collected, of which 164 participants (87 female, 76 male, 1 "not listed", Mage = 30.63, SDage = 5.36) were included in the final analysis sample.

Materials

DR Task

The DR task included 24 trials and two attention checks, with a break after 12 trials.

Apart from the attention checks, which had a fixed trial number, all trials appeared in random order. On each trial, participants read two premises, each describing "I" or "you" doing or feeling something at a certain place and time. The two premises always described a different person, place, and time. An example combination of premises could be "You were rollerblading on the sidewalk two days ago; I am stretching in the sports center right now" (see Figure 1). Half of the trials included two premises about actions (action trials), whereas the other half included two premises about feelings (emotion trials). Below the premises, participants read a reversal statement, which could include an interpersonal ("If I were you and you were me"), spatial (e.g., "If the sidewalk were the sports center, and the sports center were the sidewalk"), or temporal (e.g., "If now were two days ago and two days ago were now") deictic reversal, or a combination of two reversals (i.e., a double-reversal), resulting in six possible reversals. This created a 2-by-6 task design, in which the trial type (action trial, emotion trial) and reversal (six possible reversals) varied.

Based on the given premises and reversal statement, participants had to select all buttons with true or false statements from 2-to-4 buttons. Trials differed based on whether participants had to indicate true or false statements, the number of buttons (2, 3, 4), and the number of true (none true, one true, two true) vs. false (none false, one false, two false, three false) statements. There was always at least one correct option. If participants had not clicked the submit button before the response deadline of 80 seconds, no response was registered, and the next trial started immediately. Figure 1 provides two example trials in the DR task. Two Example Trials in the Deictic Relating Task A B

Note. Figure 1A shows an emotion trial, in which both premises are about emotions, with an interpersonal-spatial reversal. In this trial, participants must select false statements from three buttons. Figure 1B shows an action trial in the deictic relating task, in which both premises are about an action, with a spatial reversal. In this trial, participants must select true statements from four buttons. The number in the circle indicates the seconds left in the trial.

VPT Task

The VPT task (Huang et al., 2026) contained four blocks of 48 trials (192 trials).

Figure 2 shows two trials in the VPT task. Each trial started with a 700 ms inter-trial interval, showing a white "+" on a black background. After this period, participants observed an image of an avatar standing at a round table on which two balls were placed next to each other, a red and a yellow ball. Participants reacted to the left-right position of the red ball from the avatar's perspective by pressing the F-or J-key, corresponding to the responses "left" and "right" respectively. There was no response deadline, but participants were instructed to react as fast and accurately as possible. The next trial immediately started after the participant's response.

In each trial, the avatar's perspective could be congruent or incongruent with the participant's perspective. More specifically, the avatar could be placed at different angles (i.e., positions) around the table, with a 0° angle corresponding to the participant's perspective. Six Two Example Trials in the Visual Perspective-Taking Task Note. ITI stands for inter-trial interval. In the congruent trial, the avatar is standing at the left half of the table at a 22.5° angle, with balls positioned far away from them. The correct response is the J-key. In the incongruent trial, the avatar is positioned at the right half of the table, at a 157.5° angle, with the balls positioned close to them. The correct response in this trial is the F-key. The materials used in this figure were adapted with permission from Huang et al. (2026).

Multiple-Choice Faux Pas Recognition Test

We used a multiple-choice version of the Faux Pas Recognition Test, closely based on the German multiple-choice Faux Pas Recognition Test developed by Burghardt et al. (2025).

To do so, a native German speaker first translated the German task materials into English. The translations were then checked by a native English speaker, after which we adjusted some items for clarity. We further used the original stories and questions from the English openformat Faux Pas Recognition Test for adults (Stone et al., 1998), rather than the German version, which was itself a translation of the original materials. The full translation with details on changes compared to the original (English) task materials can be found on the OSF (https://osf.io/794zs/overview?view_only=3e280f4fb23f481a8ec0a5028cffa73c).

In this task, participants read 20 short stories (taken from Stone et al., 1998), presented in a fixed order: 10 stories contained a faux pas (faux pas stories) and 10 stories did not (control stories). After reading a story, participants first received a yes-no question (Q1): "In the story, did anyone say something they shouldn't have said or something awkward?" If they indicated "yes" to this question, they had to answer three additional questions, namely, (Q2) "Who said something they shouldn't have said or something awkward?", (Q3) "Why do you think he/she said it?", and (Q4) "How do you think […] felt?", in which the blank was filled in by another character in the story.

For faux pas stories, this was always the "victim" of the faux pas. If participants indicated "no" to the first question, questions 2, 3, and 4 were skipped for that story. Questions 2, 3, and 4 always had four response options. For each story, participants also completed two comprehension questions about the content of the story.

Comprehension questions could have between 2 and 4 response options. The written story remained on the screen for all questions, and participants could not go back to previous questions.

The ICAR Sample Test

The ICAR Sample Test (Condon & Revelle, 2014) is a shortened version of the ICAR Test (The International Cognitive Ability Resource Team, 2014) and includes four subscales, each including four items from the ICAR: Verbal Reasoning (items 4, 16, 17, and 19), Letter and Number Series (items 7, 33, 34, 58), Matrix Reasoning (items 45, 46, 47, 55), and Three-Dimensional Rotation (items 3, 4, 6, 8). The items were presented one by one in a fixed order.

Each item appeared on a separate screen during the experiment, and participants could not go back to previous questions.

The AQ-Short

The AQ-Short (Hoekstra et al., 2011) contains 28 items from the full AQ (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001) divided into five subscales: social skills (8 items), imagination (8 items), routines (3 items), attention to numbers and patterns (5 items), and attention switching (4 items). Participants indicated how much they agreed with each statement on a four-point Likert scale, with the options "definitely disagree", "disagree", "agree", and "definitely agree". The AQ-Short was scored following Hoekstra et al. (2011), with item scores ranging from 1 (definitely disagree) to 4 (definitely agree).

Procedure

At the start of the study, participants provided informed consent and demographic information, including age and gender ("male," "female," "non-binary," "not listed," or "prefer not to say"). Participants who selected "not listed" could specify an alternative gender.

Participants first completed the DR task, for which they first completed three practice trials with elaborate feedback for incorrect responses. After the DR task, participants completed the VPT task and Faux Pas Recognition Test, for which the order was randomized across participants. The presentation order was roughly balanced across participants, with 85 (52%) participants completing the VPT task first and 79 (48%) participants completing the Faux Pas Recognition Test first. For the VPT task, participants first completed a practice block with twelve trials, which was repeated until they had an accuracy of at least 75% (correct on 9 out of 12 trials). The Faux Pas Recognition Test did not include any practice trials. After both tasks, participants completed the ICAR Sample Test and the AQ-Short. Finally, participants were debriefed and informed that they could contact the researcher via Prolific if they had any questions or would like to receive a summary of the results. Participants were also given the option to leave a comment before finishing the study.

Analysis

All data were processed and analyzed using R (Version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2023).

Participant and trial exclusions followed the preregistered plan.

Primary Outcome Measures

The DR Task. In line with previous research, a trial in the DR task was coded as correct if all correct statements (i.e., either all false or all true statements, depending on the instruction) were selected and all incorrect statements were unselected. A trial was coded as incorrect if participants made one or more mistakes or did not press the submit button before the trial deadline. Our outcome measure for the DR task was the average accuracy across all 24 trials.

The VPT Task. As VPT tasks typically show ceiling effects on accuracy (e.g., Huang et al., 2026; Kessler & Rutherford, 2010; Michelon & Zacks, 2006), we chose to use the congruency effect on the reaction times (RTs) as our main outcome measure. This was calculated by subtracting the participant's mean RT on (correct) congruent trials from their mean RT on (correct) incongruent trials (which corresponds to the "visual congruency" effect in Huang et al., 2026). Because congruency effects often scale with general RT, it is recommended to control for overall RT to reduce the potential for misinterpreting congruency effects (Faust et al., 1999). Hence, we divided the congruency effect by the participant's overall mean RT to obtain a "relative" congruency effect for each participantfoot_2 : .

The Faux Pas Recognition Test. We based our score calculation on the study by Burghardt et al. (2025), who recommended using only the empathy and the intention scores suggested by Stone et al. (1998). To calculate a participant's score, stories with one or two incorrect comprehension questions were first excluded. The scoring of the intention and empathy questions depended on whether the participant answered the first question correctly.

For faux pas stories, the intention question was scored as correct if the participant selected the correct response on the intention question (Q3) after identifying a faux pas in Q1.

For control stories, the intention question was scored as correct if the participant correctly indicated that no faux pas had occurred in Q1, in which case Q3 was not presented. If a participant responded incorrectly to Q1, the intention question was always scored as incorrect.

The empathy question (Q4) was scored as correct if participants selected the correct response on Q4, regardless of whether they answered Q1 correctly. For control stories, the empathy question was also scored as correct if participants correctly indicated in Q1 that no faux pas had occurred, in which case Q4 was not presented. The empathy question was scored as incorrect if participants failed to identify a faux pas in Q1 for faux pas stories (resulting in Q4 not being presented) or if they selected an incorrect emotion on Q4.

Regarding the calculation of the total intention and empathy score, Burghardt et al.

(2025) recommended not dividing the total scores by the number of correctly answered comprehension questions. However, because we aimed to assess accuracy on empathy and intention questions, independent of comprehension, we chose to take the average score across all included stories (i.e., stories with correct comprehension questions). The intention score was calculated by taking the average score on the intention questions across all included stories, and the empathy score was calculated by taking the average score on all empathy questions for included stories. We used the sum of the intention and empathy score, ranging from 0 to 2, as the total score for the Faux Pas Recognition Test.

Participant and Trial Exclusion

Participant Exclusions. Only participants with complete data (> 80%) on the DR task, the VPT task, and the Faux Pas Recognition Test were included in the analysis. Eight participants were excluded because they failed more than one out of the four attention checks during the experiment. Four additional participants were excluded because they had more than 20% trials with RTs ≤ 5 seconds during the DR task (1 participant) or because their average accuracy in the VPT task was ≤ 57% (3 participants). This accuracy threshold corresponds to the 97.5th percentile of a binomial distribution with 192 trials and a success probability of 0.5, with the corresponding lower bound at 43% (2.5th percentile). Accuracy scores between these values may reflect random responding. Because the RT congruency effect on the VPT task was calculated based on correct trials only, we applied a one-sided threshold.

Trial Exclusions.

In the Faux Pas Recognition Test, all questions for a story were excluded if the participant responded incorrectly to one or more of the comprehension questions for that story (4.45% of the stories were excluded across all participants). In the VPT task, trials were excluded from all analyses if the log-transformed RT ≥ 3SD above or below the participant's average log-transformed RT (1% of trials were excluded). We used log-transformed RTs to approximate a normal distribution. VPT task trials with incorrect responses were removed for the relative RT congruency effect calculation (4.49%).

Primary Confirmatory Analyses

As preregistered, we computed Spearman's rank-ordered correlations between (H1) accuracy on the DR task and the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, and between (H2) accuracy on the DR task and the summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. We report the corresponding 95% CIs and raw p values. We computed Bayes Factors (BF) for the correlations of interest using Jeffrey's default BF hypothesis test (Ly et al., 2016), available in the BayesFactor package in R (Morey et al., 2024).

Preregistered Secondary Analyses

Difference in the Correlation Between DR and Low-vs. High-Level ToM. We tested whether the Spearman correlation between DR accuracy scores and the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task significantly differed from the correlation between the DR accuracy scores and the summed intention-empathy score, using the cocor package in R. As we aimed to test differences in strength, we aligned the correlations to the same direction by reversing negative correlations (if there were any). We expected a stronger correlation with the relative RT congruency effect compared to the summed intention-empathy score.

Correlations with the ICAR Sample Test Scores.

We computed Spearman accuracy on the DR task, their relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, and their summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.

correlations between participants' average accuracy on the ICAR Sample Test and their

We report adjusted p values and corrected 95% CIs using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure for controlling the False Discovery Rate (FDR).

Correlations with AQ-Short Scores.

Finally, we also computed Spearman correlations between participants' AQ-Short scores and their accuracy on the DR task, their relative VPT RT congruency effect, and their summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. We report adjusted p values and corrected 95% CIs using the BH procedure.

We preregistered that we would also calculate the correlations between AQ scores and all specific Faux Pas Recognition Test scores, for which the analysis and results can be found in the Supplementary Materials (Appendix A).

Results

Task Performance and Reliability

The DR Task

Participants had an average score of 60.47% (SD = 24.39%) on the DR task. Using the SplitHalf function in the Psych package in R, the average split-half reliability (across 10,000 iterations) for the DR task was estimated at r = .88, 95% CI [.84, .91].

The VPT task

The average accuracy on the VPT task was 95.51% (SD = 5.49%). Participants showed a significant relative RT congruency effect, t(163) = 19.17, p < .001, and accuracy congruency effect, t(163) = 9.01, p < .001. Participants were faster (Mraw RT difference = 358 ms, SD = 527 ms) and more accurate (Mdifference = 6.75%, SD = 9.59%) on congruent compared to incongruent trials. The average Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability for the relative RT congruency effect (across 10,000 iterations) was estimated at r = .93, 95% CI [.90, .95].

The Faux Pas Recognition Test

The average accuracies on the intention and empathy questions were 81.12% (SD = 13.05) and 79.40% (SD = 11.48%), respectively, based on stories with correct comprehension questions. Using the function in the Psych package, the average split-half reliability (across 10,000 iterations) of the summed intention-empathy score was estimated at r = .60, 95% CI [.47, .70].

ICAR Sample Test

Participants had an average accuracy of 55.26% (SD = 19.69%) on the ICAR Sample Test. We calculated the stratified Cronbach's alpha (αstratified; Cronbach et al., 1965), as the ICAR Sample Test contains different subscales, using the sirt package in R, together with a bootstrapped CI (across 10,000 iterations). Internal consistency was acceptable, αstratified = .77 (16 items), 95% CI [.71, .82].

The AQ-Short

Using dimensional scoring, the total AQ-Short scores ranged from 40 to 107 (M = 64.58, SD = 11.93) on 112. The AQ-Short showed good internal consistency, αstratified = .89 (28 items), 95% CI [.85, .91]. Forty-six (28.05%) participants scored equal to or above the (stringent) cut-off of 70/112 proposed by Hoekstra et al. (2011).

Primary Confirmatory Analyses

Correlation of DR Accuracy Scores and Relative VPT RT Congruency Effect

In contrast to H1, participants' accuracy on the DR task was not significantly correlated with their relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, r(162) = .05, p = .512, 95% CI [-.10, .20]. The BF analysis provided evidence for the absence of a correlation, BF10 = 0.22, with the data being 4.49 times more likely in the absence of a correlation. Figure 3A represents the scatterplot for DR accuracy and the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task.

Correlation of DR Accuracy Scores and Summed Intention-Empathy Scores

In line with H2, there was a significant, positive correlation between accuracy scores on the DR task and the summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, r(162) = .44, p < .001, 95% CI [.31, .56]. The BF analysis provided evidence for the presence of a correlation, with the data being 5,336,603 times more likely under a model that assumes a correlation. Figure 3B represents the scatterplot for DR accuracy and the summed intentionempathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.
