Preregistered Secondary Analysis

Difference in the Correlation Between DR and Low-vs. High-Level ToM

The correlation between the accuracy on the DR task and the summed intentionempathy score was significantly larger than the correlation with the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, z = -3.85, p < .001, which was not in line with our prediction based on RFT that DR would correlate more strongly with low-than high-level ToM.

Correlations with ICAR Sample Test Scores

Participants' average accuracy on the ICAR Sample Test correlated significantly with their accuracy on the DR task, r(162) = .56, padj < .001, 95% CIadj [.42, .68], and with the summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, r(162) = .36, padj < .001, 95% CIadj [.18, .51]. There was no significant correlation between ICAR Sample Test scores and the relative RT congruency effects, r(162) = -.08, padj = .295, 95% CIadj [-.26, .11].

Correlations with AQ-Short Scores

Participants' AQ-Short scores were significantly positively correlated with accuracy on the DR task, r(162) = .19, padj = .048, 95% CIadj [.00, .36]. This association indicates that participants with more autism traits had higher accuracy on DR, contrary to our predictions.

The correlations of AQ-Short scores with the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, r(162) = -.09, padj = .236, 95% CIadj [-.27, .10], and with the summed intention-empathy score, r(162) = .16, padj = .055, 95% CIadj [-.02, .34], were not significant after BH correction.

Post-Hoc Analyses

Partial Correlation Between the Summed Intention-Empathy Score and DR task, Controlled for ICAR Sample Test Scores

Because both the accuracy on the DR task and the ICAR Sample Test correlated positively with the summed intention-empathy score, we tested whether the correlation of the summed intention-empathy score with the DR task remained significant after controlling for ICAR Sample Test scores, using the ppcor package for partial correlations in R. According to RFT, DR should relate to ToM beyond general cognitive ability; hence, the correlation with DR accuracy should remain significant after filtering out variance related to ICAR scores.

This analysis revealed a significant partial Spearman correlation between the summed intention-empathy score and the DR task, controlling for ICAR scores, r(161) = .32, p < .001, 95% CI [.17, .45].

Correlations with the VPT Accuracy Congruency Effect

Because the outcome measures of the DR task and ICAR Sample Test were accuracybased, we also computed correlations between these tasks and the accuracy congruency effect in the VPT task, for which we adjusted p values and 95% CIs using the BH procedure. This post-hoc analysis revealed a significant negative correlation between the accuracy congruency effect and DR task accuracy, r(162) = -.19, padj = .013, 95% CIadj [-.36, -.02], and ICAR Sample Test scores, r(162) = -.24, padj = .004, 95% CIadj

Discussion

Previous research on the relationship between DR and ToM has been mixed, potentially due to small sample sizes (e.g., Jackson et al., 2014; Weil et al., 2011) and the limited applicability of the Barnes-Holmes protocol for adults (Kavanagh et al., 2020). The current study tested correlations between performance on a recently developed DR task suitable for adults and a low-and high-level ToM task, namely a VPT task and the Faux Pas Recognition Test, in a large general population sample. We further tested correlations with a measure of cognitive abilities, the ICAR Sample Test, and a self-report questionnaire of autism traits, the AQ-Short. Contrary to H1, DR performance was not significantly correlated with our low-level ToM measure, the RT congruency effect in the VPT task. However, DR was significantly correlated with our high-level ToM measure, the summed intention-empathy score, consistent with H2. The correlation with high-level ToM was significantly stronger than with low-level ToM, which was opposite to what would be predicted by RFT. In a secondary analysis, we found significant correlations of the ICAR Sample Test with both DR and the summed intention-empathy scores. Furthermore, autism traits were positively correlated with DR, although they were not significantly correlated with the summed intention-empathy scores and VPT RT congruency effect. Hence, contrary to our predictions, higher autism trait scores were associated with higher accuracy on the DR task, and were not significantly associated with performance on our ToM tasks. Because the summed intention-empathy score correlated with both DR and ICAR scores, and RFT predicts that DR should relate to Faux Pas performance beyond general cognitive ability, we conducted a post-hoc analysis to test whether DR scores still correlated with the summed intention-empathy scores when controlling for ICAR scores. In line with RFT's prediction, the analysis revealed a significant partial correlation between DR and summed intention-empathy scores after controlling for ICAR scores. This suggests that the relation between DR and performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test cannot be fully explained by general cognitive ability.

Regarding H1, a possible explanation for the absence of a significant correlation with VPT is that this was the only outcome based on RTs, whereas the other outcome measures were accuracy scores. To test this, we performed a post-hoc correlational analysis with the accuracy congruency effect instead of the RT congruency effect. This analysis revealed small but significant negative correlations with DR and ICAR scores. That is, higher DR and ICAR scores were related to smaller accuracy congruency effects in the VPT task. The negative correlation with DR is in line with RFT's prediction, as the congruency effect reflects a cost for perspective switching (i.e., lower accuracy for incongruent vs. congruent perspectives); a smaller congruency effect therefore indicates less difficulty with switching perspectives.

However, the non-significant partial correlation between DR and VPT after controlling for ICAR scores suggests that the observed correlation with the DR task may reflect general cognitive ability rather than a specific link between DR and VPT. The absence of a unique association aligns with Taylor et al. (2023), who found no effect of DR training on VPT performance; if observed associations are solely driven by cognitive ability, specific DR training is unlikely to transfer to VPT. Moreover, RFT further assumes low-level ToM to rely more directly on DR compared to high-level ToM (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Kavanagh et al., 2020). Hence, these findings for low-level ToM are at odds with RFT's predictions.

However, we did find a correlation between DR and high-level ToM. The observed correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test is consistent with previous correlational research reporting correlations between DR and vignette-based high-level ToM tasks (Hendriks et al., 2016; Villatte et al., 2008 Villatte et al., , 2010)). However, several alternative explanations for the relationship between the two tasks must be considered. First, we observed a stronger correlation between DR and high-level ToM compared to low-level ToM.

Importantly, our low-and high-level ToM tasks differed not only in ToM level but also in task format: the VPT task was non-verbal, whereas both the DR and Faux Pas Recognition

Test were text-based. Moreover, the Faux Pas Recognition Test and DR task both rely on active reasoning (i.e., reading certain statements or stories, and answering questions about their content), which is likely more cognitively demanding than simply overcoming one's own visual perspective in a two-choice, trial-based task. Hence, the relationship between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test may partly reflect shared task characteristics and reliance on active reasoning rather than a link between DR and ToM abilities. Using the same logic, it is also possible that DR did not significantly correlate with VPT (beyond cognitive ability) because these tasks differ (too much) in format. Therefore, task-specific variance may have obscured a potential association between VPT and DR. To investigate task-specific influences, future research could include tasks with other task formats, such as a non-verbal high-level ToM task (e.g., Nijhof et al., 2017), or add a cognitive non-social task with overlapping task structure and difficulty.

Relatedly, because of the overlap in task structure, the observed correlation may (partly) reflect a third underlying ability assessed in both the DR task and the Faux Pas Recognition Test other than perspective-taking. One possibility is verbal ability, as language skills have been linked to ToM performance (Astington & Jenkins, 1999; Milligan et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2021) as well as DR (Gore et al., 2010). Moreover, RFT states that relational responding is essential to language development (Hayes et al., 2001), and critiques of DR have argued that the Barnes-Holmes protocol may function as training in complex sentence structures rather than perspective-taking (Taylor & Edwards, 2021). Although the ICAR Sample Test includes a verbal reasoning subscale, it comprises only four items and may therefore provide a limited assessment of verbal ability. Hence, whereas ICAR scores did not fully explain the correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test, a more comprehensive test of verbal ability might. These alternative explanations of the observed correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test are not only relevant to the current study, but may also explain previously reported correlations between performance on the Barnes-Holmes protocol and vignette-based ToM tasks (Hendriks et al., 2016; Villatte et al., 2008 Villatte et al., , 2010)). Future research could include a more comprehensive measure of language skills to determine whether the observed association persists when taking into account verbal ability.

It is also possible that the observed correlation reflects a relationship between ToM and relational responding more generally, rather than a specific association with DR. Because DR is thought to be specifically related to ToM development, ToM should show a stronger association with DR than with other relational frames. To test the specificity of the relationship, future studies could include additional measures of (non-deictic) relational responding. One measure could be the analogy subscale in the improved Relational Abilities Index (J. Cummins & J. De Houwer, personal communication, June 2024; Nevejans et al., 2026), which closely matches the DR task in structure and difficulty. If ToM correlates more strongly with DR than with other relational frames, this would provide stronger evidence that its correlation is not solely based on relational abilities in general or overlap in task structure.

Regarding our secondary analysis, the lack of a significant correlation between the summed intention-empathy score and autism traits was unexpected, given that the ToM account of autism predicts lower scores (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985), a prediction that was supported by previous findings on autism traits and ToM (Atherton & Cross, 2019; Gökçen et al., 2016; Nijhof et al., 2017). However, not all previous studies have found ToM difficulties in autism (for a critical review, see Gernsbacher & Yergeau, 2019; Loukusa et al., 2023), and several authors have raised issues with the ToM hypothesis in autism (e.g., Long et al., 2025; Milton, 2012) and the validity of ToM tasks more generally (Long et al., 2025; Quesque & Rossetti, 2020). Note that our Faux Pas Recognition Test was a translation of the German multiple-choice version of the test, which focused on clinical groups other than autism (Burghardt et al., 2025), whereas the original task was open-format (Stone et al., 1998). These changes may have influenced the task's relevance for autism. Nevertheless, our findings contribute to the broader discussion about whether such ToM tasks measure important reallife social abilities that are different in autism (Long et al., 2025; Quesque & Rossetti, 2020).

Another unexpected finding is the positive correlation between autism traits and DR.

Based on the RFT, one would expect a negative correlation, namely that people with more autism traits would perform worse on DR (Kavanagh et al., 2020; Rehfeldt et al., 2007). In a previous study, we did not observe a significant correlation between DR and the full AQ in a large general adult sample (Nevejans et al., 2026). Because both this study and Experiment 2 in our previous study included a DR task and AQ, we performed a post-hoc random-effects meta-analysis, combining AQ-Short and DR task scores from both studies (Ntotal = 284; see Appendix C for full analysis and results). This analysis revealed a significant meta-analytic positive correlation across studies (r = .17, p = .004). Because this suggests that higher autism scores are associated with better DR performance, our results raise doubts about the proposal that autism is linked to poorer DR performance (e.g., Rehfeldt et al., 2007) and that training DR may serve as a useful intervention strategy (e.g., Belisle et al., 2016; Gilroy et al., 2015; Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014).

However, generalization of these results to autism is limited, as we assessed autism traits in a general population sample. Although many participants scored above the AQ-Short cut-off score (28%), which may indicate eligibility for a diagnosis of autism, we cannot generalize these findings to individuals with formal autism diagnoses, especially since the AQ-Short was primarily developed for research purposes and is not a diagnostic instrument.

Although a higher percentage than the actual prevalence rate is to be expected when sensitivity is prioritized, the observed percentage of participants exceeding the cut-off is notably higher than the estimated prevalence of autism in the general population (1%; Zeidan et al., 2022). In our previous research using Prolific samples, up to 11% of participants also scored above the 50-item AQ cut-off (Nevejans et al., 2026; Experiment 1), suggesting a possible selection bias toward individuals with elevated autism traits on Prolific, at least for this type of research. This warrants further investigation; nevertheless, it resulted in sufficient variation in autism traits for our correlational analyses.

To conclude, we found a relationship between DR and high-level ToM (i.e., the summed intention-empathy score), but only a weak relationship between DR and low-level ToM in a post-hoc analysis, and the latter correlation disappeared when controlling for general cognitive ability. Although these findings could suggest a relationship between DR and ToM, they are at odds with RFT. Since RFT positions DR as the functional prerequisite for all perspective-taking, an association with high-level ToM that bypasses low-level ToM challenges the theory's hierarchical prediction that DR directly supports the most basic levels of ToM, whereas high-level ToM might require additional skills (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Kavanagh et al., 2020). Moreover, it could be that observed correlations between DR and vignette-based high-level ToM tasks depend on shared task characteristics, or other influential factors in the included tasks, rather than a link between DR and ToM abilities. Future research should test whether the relationship between DR and ToM remains when controlling for the (verbal) format of the tasks, and for other relevant abilities, such as verbal ability or relational responding more generally. If not, the shared variance might simply reflect other cognitive skills or effort. Notably, DR showed a small but positive correlation with autism traits across two studies (see Appendix B), indicating that individuals with higher autism trait scores performed better on this task, which is a finding opposite to our expectation and questions whether training DR in autism is a useful intervention strategy. Typically, RFT predicts that autism traits should be associated with lower performance, not advantages, in the relational framing skills that are supposed to underpin perspective-taking. Moreover, performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test did not show any relation to autism traits, which raises questions about its usefulness to autism research on social abilities. Hence, future research should assess how performance on these tasks relates to real-life social skills and whether they are relevant for the social difficulties reported by individuals with autism.

Both the current study and one of the experiments (Experiment 2) in a previous study included the deictic relating task and the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ). Data Accessibility

Experiment materials (excluding copyrighted measures: Faux Pas Recognition Test stories and ICAR materials), data and analysis code (in R) are available on the Open Science Framework: https://osf.io/794zs/overview?view_only=3e280f4fb23f481a8ec0a5028cffa73c.

Supplementary Materials Appendix A: Correlations between the AQ-short and specific Faux Pas Recognition Test scores.

Note. We preregistered that we would also test correlations between the short Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-Short) scores and the different scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. The analysis details and results are included in this Appendix.

Analysis

As the Faux Pas Recognition Test includes different scores, we also computed correlations between the scores on the AQ-Short (Hoekstra et al., 2011) and three specific scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test: the detection score, the intention score, and the empathy score. We expected a negative correlation between AQ-Short scores and all the different scores. The calculations for the faux pas intention and empathy score were described in the manuscript.

For the calculation of the detection score, stories with one or two incorrect comprehension questions are again excluded. For faux pas stories, (correct) answers to the first and second questions were summed (i.e., a maximum of 2 points per story). Note that, if the first question was answered incorrectly, the second question was not shown and received a zero score as well. For control stories, if the participant answered the first question correctly, they received 2 points. If not, they receive zero points. In line with Stone et al. (1998), we calculated the mean detection score across all included stories.

We computed Spearman's rank-ordered correlations between participants' AQ-Short scores and their detection, intention, and empathy scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.

We report adjusted p values and 95% CIs corrected using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure for controlling the False Discovery Rate.

Appendix B: Meta-analysis on the relation between autism traits and performance on deictic relating.

Note. Both the current study and one of the experiments (Experiment 2) in a previous study included the deictic relating task and the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ). Therefore, we conducted an exploratory cross-study random-effects meta-analysis to more robustly assess the relationship between deictic relating and autism traits across our two experiments (Ntotal = 284). The analysis details and results can be found in this Appendix.

Analysis

We first calculated AQ-Short scores and accuracy scores on the deictic relating task with 24 trials based on the data from Nevejans et al. (2026), which included the full 50-item AQ and a deictic relating task with 48 trials. For the AQ, we omitted items that are not included in the AQ-short and recalculated the total AQ-Short score. For the deictic relating task in the previous experiment, we removed trials with a repetition of information, as these trials were not included in the 24-trial version used in the current study (for more information, see Experiment 2 of Nevejans et al., 2026). This ensured identical outcome measures for both studies (but note that results are similar for including the full 48-trial version of the deictic relating task). The random-effects meta-analysis was conducted based on Fisher's ztransformed correlation statistic, using the metacor function from the meta package in R (Schwarzer et al., 2015).

Results

We found a significant meta-analytic correlation between the AQ-Short scores and performance on the deictic relating task across experiments, k = 2, z = 2.88, p = .004, with a corresponding re-transformed Spearman correlation coefficient of r = .17, 95% CI [.06, .28].

There was no significant heterogeneity of the effect between the two experiments, Q(1) = 0.11, p = .737.

Apart from the angle, trials differed on the positioning of the red ball (left vs. right), the distance of the balls from the avatar (close, far), and the left-right position of the avatar at the table (left half of the table, right half of the table). This created 48 different trial conditions, each appearing once during each block. After each block, participants were informed about their average accuracy in the finished block.

Contrary to the prediction based on RFT, the partial correlation between DR scores and the VPT accuracy congruency effect was non-significant after controlling for ICAR scores, r(161) = -.07, p = .351, 95% CI [-.22, .08].

In this manuscript, we chose to use an abbreviated version of the diagnostic term and refer to a person with an autism spectrum disorder diagnosis as a person with autism. With this, we do not intend to take a stance in the ongoing person-first versus identity-first debate, in which there is currently no consensus(Flowers et al., 2023).

With this note, we aim to acknowledge and respect different language preferences(De Laet et al., 2025).

Other methods for controlling RTs exist, such as taking the natural logarithm of RTs. Using the congruency effect on the log-transformed RTs in the main analyses produced similar results as for the relative congruency effect and therefore does not change the conclusions.

Results Participants' AQ-short scores were not significantly correlated with any of the scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, all r ≤ .14, all padj ≥ .107, after BH correction. Note that these correlations were also non-significant without correction, all praw ≥ .069. Appendix References
